blogs.title: The "Instigation" Problem: When Secondary Users Manufacture the Original Work
blogs.description: This post examines Santos's novel argument that Kimmel's fair use defense should fail because Kimmel "instigated" the creation of the copyrighted videos through his Cameo requests. The court's rejection of this theory reaffirms that transformativeness is judged by what a "reasonable observer" perceives, not by the subjective intent of either party. This ruling clarifies that even when a secondary user solicits creation of an original work, the transformative use inquiry remains objective—focusing on whether the secondary use adds new meaning or purpose, not on who set the original work in motion.

blogs.title: Whatever Happened to Good Faith? The Continuing Erosion of Harper & Row's Moral Dimension
blogs.description: Santos argued that Kimmel's deception—using fictitious names to solicit Cameo videos—constituted bad faith that should preclude fair use. The Second Circuit's response is striking: it notes that the Supreme Court has "distanced itself" from Harper & Row's famous pronouncement that "fair use presupposes good faith and fair dealing." This post analyzes the doctrinal drift away from treating bad faith as a fair use disqualifier and asks whether deceptive acquisition of copyrighted material should matter more in the fair use calculus, particularly in an era of AI scraping and platform manipulation.

blogs.title: Dodging Preemption: Strategic Avoidance of the Copyright Preemption Question
blogs.description: The District Court held Santos's contract claims were preempted by the Copyright Act. The Second Circuit affirmed on alternative grounds—finding each state law claim failed on its own merits under state contract and fraud principles. This post explores the strategic and doctrinal implications of courts avoiding copyright preemption questions, examining why courts sometimes prefer to resolve cases on state law grounds and what litigants should take away from this approach when pleading around copyright claims.

blogs.title: Platform Terms of Service and the Third-Party Beneficiary Problem: Who Can Enforce the Contract?
blogs.description: Santos sought to enforce Cameo's Terms of Service against Kimmel, but the court held Santos was not a party to that contract and lacked third-party beneficiary status under Illinois law. This post analyzes the implications for gig economy workers and platform users who rely on platform terms to protect their interests, examining the high bar for third-party beneficiary status when platforms' own terms selectively provide such rights in some provisions but not others.
